summary: Dexketoprofen is the pharmacologically active S(+)-enantiomer of ketoprofen, a propionic-acid NSAID used for short-term symptomatic relief of mild to moderate acute pain (e.g., musculoskeletal pain, dysmenorrhea, dental and postoperative pain). It has a rapid onset and short half-life, allowing lower total NSAID exposure than racemic ketoprofen. It is approved in Europe and many other regions but is NOT FDA-approved in the United States.
indications: Short-term symptomatic treatment of mild to moderate acute pain
Postoperative pain (including parenteral form where available)

moa: Dexketoprofen is the active S(+)-enantiomer of ketoprofen. It non-selectively inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2), reducing the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins. Decreased prostaglandin synthesis at peripheral and central sites produces analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antipyretic effects.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to dexketoprofen, ketoprofen, or other NSAIDs/salicylates
History of asthma, bronchospasm, urticaria or angioedema precipitated by NSAIDs/aspirin
Active or history of recurrent peptic ulcer / GI bleeding
Active GI bleeding or other active bleeding
relative: History of GI disease, Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis
Mild-moderate hepatic or mild renal impairment
Concomitant medicines increasing bleeding or GI risk
monitor: Diuretics, ACE inhibitors or ARBs (renal risk)
Patients with fluid retention, hypertension or cardiovascular risk factors

preg: Avoid in the first and second trimesters unless clearly necessary. Contraindicated from around 20-28 weeks gestation onward and in the third trimester due to risks of premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, fetal renal impairment/oligohydramnios, and inhibition of labour. May impair female fertility and is not recommended in women attempting to conceive.
lact: There are no data on excretion of dexketoprofen in human milk. Use during breastfeeding is not recommended; avoid.
renal: Contraindicated in moderate to severe renal impairment. In mild renal impairment, limit total dose to 50 mg/day. NSAIDs can reduce renal perfusion and precipitate acute kidney injury, especially with dehydration, diuretics, ACE inhibitors or ARBs.
hepatic: Limit total dose to 50 mg/day in mild to moderate hepatic impairment with close monitoring. Contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C). Discontinue if liver function tests are persistently abnormal or signs of liver disease develop.

major: Other NSAIDs including high-dose aspirin and COX-2 inhibitors - increased GI bleeding/ulceration risk
Anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin, DOACs) - increased bleeding risk
Lithium - reduced lithium clearance, risk of toxicity
Methotrexate (high dose) - reduced clearance, increased toxicity
moderate: Diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs - reduced efficacy and increased risk of renal impairment ('triple whammy')
Antiplatelets and SSRIs - increased GI bleeding
minor: Cardiac glycosides (digoxin) - may raise plasma levels
interactions.food: Food delays absorption and onset; take with food to reduce GI upset.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - increases risk of gastrointestinal bleeding.
interactions.diagnostics: May affect renal function tests and reduce platelet aggregation; can mask fever/inflammation.

serious: Cardiovascular thrombotic events (MI, stroke) with prolonged/high-dose use
rare: Severe cutaneous reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis)

monitoring: Blood pressure at baseline and during treatment
Renal function, particularly in elderly or those on diuretics/ACE inhibitors/ARBs
Signs and symptoms of GI bleeding (especially elderly, ulcer history)
Liver function with prolonged use or if symptoms suggest hepatotoxicity
Full blood count with prolonged therapy
counsel: Use for the shortest time needed to control pain
Take with or after food to reduce stomach upset
Stop and seek help for black/tarry stools, vomiting blood, severe stomach pain, or signs of allergic reaction
Avoid combining with other NSAIDs or aspirin and limit alcohol
Tell your doctor if you have heart, kidney, liver disease, or are pregnant/breastfeeding
Report any rash or skin reaction promptly (risk of photosensitivity)

Peak plasma concentration ~0.25-0.75 hours (delayed by food)

pearls: NOT FDA-approved in the United States; licensed in Europe (EMA/national SmPC), UK (BNF) and many other countries - dosing here is based on SmPC/BNF, not FDA labeling
Dexketoprofen is the active S(+)-enantiomer of ketoprofen, so the effective dose is roughly half that of racemic ketoprofen
Rapid onset and short half-life make it suited to short-term acute pain rather than chronic inflammatory conditions
Available as dexketoprofen trometamol salt, which improves solubility and speeds absorption
Carries the usual NSAID cardiovascular, GI and renal warnings; use lowest effective dose for shortest duration
missed: As dexketoprofen is taken as needed for pain, take a dose only when required and do not exceed the maximum of 75 mg in 24 hours. If on a scheduled regimen, take a missed dose when remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose; never double up.
overdose: Symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness, headache, and in severe cases GI bleeding, hypotension, renal failure, metabolic acidosis, seizures and CNS depression. Management is supportive: consider activated charcoal if presenting within 1 hour, protect the airway, monitor cardiovascular and renal function, correct electrolytes, and give symptomatic GI protection. Dexketoprofen may be removed by dialysis. There is no specific antidote.
